title: Generating Reading Comprehension Exercises with Large Language Models for Educational Applications
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of automatically generating English reading comprehension exercises with large language models for educational use. The authors argue that prior work on LLMs in education has emphasized instructional support and writing correction more than the creation of assessment content, especially reading comprehension materials. Their goal is to build a scalable system that can produce coherent, pedagogically aligned, and personalized reading exercises including passages, questions, options, answers, and explanations.

The paper proposes a framework called Reading Comprehension Exercise Generation (RCEG). The approach combines supervised fine-tuning on reading-comprehension data, reward modeling, and reinforcement learning with proximal policy optimization to align model outputs with instructional goals. It then adds post-processing modules: Dynamic Attribute Graphs-based controlled text generation (DATG) to guide outputs toward desirable attributes, and a GeDi-based toxicity classifier to rerank and filter candidates. The system is evaluated primarily with NLP benchmarks such as BLEU, ROUGE, perplexity, FreeEval reasoning scores, and toxicity-related filtering rather than student learning outcomes.

The empirical context is educational content generation rather than a classroom intervention trial. The datasets are drawn from the RACE dataset, Gaokao English examinations, and Postgraduate English Entrance Examinations, which implies a focus on secondary-school and exam-oriented reading materials. The paper also mentions a Gradio interface intended for practical use by students and teachers, but no human participants are enrolled in an instructional effectiveness study, and no direct literacy outcomes are measured.

The main conclusion is that RCEG improves the quality of generated reading comprehension exercises compared with baseline language models. The authors report gains in BLEU/ROUGE-based similarity, some reasoning benchmarks, and lower perplexity under both standard and toxic-input conditions. They conclude that the framework shows promise for scalable educational content generation and intelligent education systems, while noting future work on dialogue generation, domain adaptation, and classroom deployment.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a technical system paper evaluating generated-content quality, not a causal or quasi-experimental study of K-12 learners. It provides no business-as-usual or non-AI student-learning comparison, no participant-level educational design, and appears to be an arXiv preprint rather than established peer-reviewed impact evidence.
impact_tier_rationale: The system shows promising improvements in generated reading-exercise quality and likely efficiency, but there is no direct evidence that it improves student literacy achievement, engagement, or other K-12 outcomes. As a result, educational impact is unclear rather than demonstrated as null or negative.

interventions.use_case: LLM-based generation of English reading comprehension exercises, including passages, questions, options, answers, and explanations, using a fine-tuned/reinforcement-learned model with controlled decoding and discriminator reranking.

finding.finding_summary: The proposed RCEG framework improved the quality of generated reading-comprehension materials relative to base models on text-similarity and quality-related benchmarks. For example, RCEG-SPQwen2.5-3B achieved BLEU-4=27.23 versus 24.24 for the base model and ROUGE-1=22.12 versus 21.80; RCEG-SPQwen2.5-7B achieved BLEU-4=39.52 versus 38.01. However, these are model-generation quality metrics on constructed datasets rather than causal evidence of improved K-12 student literacy outcomes.
finding.measure: BLEU-4, ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, ROUGE-L on generated reading comprehension exercise outputs

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that RCEG can automatically generate personalized, high-quality reading comprehension exercises and provide question resources for educators, implying improved content-production efficiency versus traditional teacher-authored exercise design. The evidence consists of system demonstrations and output-quality benchmarks, not direct measurements of teacher time saved, productivity gains, or classroom implementation outcomes.
finding.measure: Automated content generation performance; interactive system demonstration; no direct productivity metric reported
